nodes.label: Cleaver (1972) described variants of xeroderma pigmentosum that had normal DNA repair and normal sensitivity to ultraviolet light.

Lehmann et al. (1975) found that cells from the class of xeroderma pigmentosum patients whose excision repair of UV-induced pyrimidine dimers was completely normal (XP variants) had an abnormality in DNA synthesis after UV irradiation. These variant cells took much longer than normal cells to convert the low-molecular-weight DNA first made after UV irradiation into high-molecular-weight DNA.

Lehmann et al. (1975) showed that caffeine strongly inhibited the slow conversion of newly made low-molecular-weight DNA to high-molecular-weight DNA in UV-irradiated XP variant cells, but had no effect in normal cells. Two excision-repair-deficient XP cell lines showed intermediate effects, both in the time needed for this conversion and in how much caffeine inhibited it.

Cleaver et al. (1980) found that a pigmented xerodermoid cell culture could not be told apart from the XP variant in UV-irradiation studies of DNA repair and replication. They concluded that the term 'pigmented xerodermoid', which had been defined by mild clinical symptoms, was therefore redundant.

Cleaver et al. (1980) irradiated XP variant and pigmented xerodermoid cells with UV light. They measured unscheduled DNA synthesis, strand breakage during repair, chain growth during semiconservative replication with or without caffeine, and recovery of DNA replication. The authors concluded that the common defect appeared to be loss of a gene product that lets normal cells replicate DNA without interruption at UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. As a result, replication forks were blocked more often and at lower doses in XP variant cells. They suggested that this defect correlated with the high levels of actinic carcinogenesis seen in these patients.

Fujiwara et al. (1981) described an 8-year-old boy (patient UV81KO) who had only acute recurrent sunburns, with no other physical or neuromental retardation. His skin had lowered minimal erythema doses at monochromatic wavelengths between 280 and 300 nm, without delayed peaking of erythema.

Fujiwara et al. (1981) found that the patient's cultured skin fibroblasts were 5-fold more sensitive than normal cells to killing by 254-nm UV, and were also more sensitive to sunlamp UV-B, 4-nitroquinoline-1-oxide and N-hydroxy-acetylaminofluorene. The cells were not more sensitive to mitomycin C or to alkylating agents. Cells from obligate heterozygotes responded normally.

Fujiwara et al. (1981) found no detectable defect in nucleotide excision repair or replicative bypass in the patient's cells. Despite this, the cells failed to recover DNA synthesis after 254-nm UV doses of 1 and 5 J/m2, doses at which normal cells recovered. Baseline sister chromatid exchanges were raised (10 to 12 per cell versus 5 per cell in normal cells), but the rate of UV-induced exchanges was normal.

Fujiwara et al. (1981) compared the patient's features with those of xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, the 11961 disorder and Bloom syndrome. They concluded that the UV81KO disorder was distinct from all of these and proposed it as a new photodermatosis with a defect in the recovery of DNA synthesis after UV exposure.

Wang et al. (1991) stated that patients with xeroderma pigmentosum variant show the clinical features of XP, including more frequent skin cancer. Their cells have a normal or nearly normal rate of nucleotide excision repair of UV-induced DNA damage. The cells are only slightly more sensitive than normal cells to the cytotoxic effect of UV radiation but are significantly more sensitive to its mutagenic effect.

Wang et al. (1991) transfected an XP variant cell line with a supF shuttle vector plasmid irradiated with UV at 254 nm. Mutant frequency rose linearly with dose, with a slope 5 times steeper than previously seen in normal cells. In 52 of 53 independent mutants the change was a base substitution, and 62 of 64 substitutions involved a dipyrimidine. A.T base pairs were involved in 28% of mutations in XP variant cells versus 11% in normal cells, mostly at position 136. The authors suggested that XP variant cells are less likely than normal cells to incorporate dAMP opposite photoproducts, which could account for their UV hypermutability.

Itoh et al. (1996) described a simple autoradiographic method for diagnosing xeroderma pigmentosum variant that measures 3 cellular DNA repair markers after UV irradiation: unscheduled DNA synthesis (UDS), recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis. Patient fibroblasts were plated on coverslips alongside normal control cells, and grain counts on nuclei were compared. Among hereditary photosensitive disorders (XP, Cockayne syndrome, and UV-sensitive syndrome), only XP variant cells showed normal UDS and normal recovery of RNA synthesis but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis (about 50% of control), and caffeine made this reduction greater.

Itoh et al. (1996) noted that because xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome, and UV-sensitive syndrome each produce a different combination of the 3 markers, the method also gives a systematic basis for diagnosing these disorders. Before this method, XP variant had been diagnosed using a post-replication repair assay together with clinical features.

Masutani et al. (1999) noted that xeroderma pigmentosum variant (XP-V) is an inherited disorder associated with increased incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers. Unlike cells from XP groups A to G, XP-V cells carry out normal nucleotide-excision repair but are defective in replicating ultraviolet-damaged DNA.

Masutani et al. (1999) had used an improved cell-free assay to isolate a DNA polymerase from HeLa cells that, in XP-V cell extracts, continued replication on damaged DNA by bypassing ultraviolet-induced thymine dimers. They showed that this polymerase is a human homolog of yeast Rad30 (DNA polymerase eta). It belongs to a family of damage-bypass replication proteins that also includes E. coli UmuC and DinB and yeast Rev1.

Masutani et al. (1999) found mutations in the DNA polymerase eta gene (POLH) in all XP-V cells they examined. Recombinant human DNA polymerase eta corrected the inability of XP-V cell extracts to replicate damaged DNA by bypassing thymine dimers. The authors concluded that DNA polymerase eta could be the XPV gene product.

Johnson et al. (1999) found nonsense or frameshift mutations in hRAD30, the human counterpart of the yeast RAD30 gene, in XP variant (XP-V) cell lines. Of the 8 mutations identified, 7 were predicted to result in a severely truncated hRad30 protein. The authors concluded that defects in hRAD30 cause XP-V.

Johnson et al. (1999) noted that yeast RAD30 encodes a DNA polymerase involved in error-free bypass of UV damage, and suggested that error-free replication of UV lesions by hRad30 plays an important role in minimizing the incidence of sunlight-induced skin cancers.

Itoh et al. (2000) noted that, among hereditary photosensitive disorders including other XP groups, Cockayne syndrome, and UV-sensitive syndrome, only XPV cells showed normal unscheduled DNA synthesis and normal recovery of RNA synthesis but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis after UV irradiation (51 +/- 6% of normal), a reduction enhanced to 36 +/- 5% in the presence of a nontoxic level of caffeine.

Itoh et al. (2000) studied 2 independent families with 2 photosensitive patients identified as having XPV. Cells from heterozygous parents showed normal unscheduled DNA synthesis, recovery of RNA synthesis, and recovery of replicative DNA synthesis, but reduced recovery of replicative DNA synthesis in the presence of 1 mM caffeine (53 +/- 8% of normal), and normal UV survival without caffeine but slightly reduced survival with caffeine in a colony-forming assay. The authors suggested that XPV heterozygotes can be identified by UV sensitivity in the presence of nontoxic caffeine.

In 1 family with XPV, Itoh et al. (2000) confirmed inheritance of 2 heterozygous missense mutations: an A-to-G transition at nucleotide 1840 resulting in a lys535-to-glu (K535E) substitution, and an A-to-C transversion at nucleotide 2003 affecting lys589. Neither mutation was found in 52 unrelated Japanese individuals.

Using DNA combing, Despras et al. (2010) showed that the translesion synthesis defect in UV-irradiated XP-V cells, which lack DNA polymerase eta, caused a strong reduction in the number of active replication forks and a high proportion of stalled forks. This contrasted with budding yeast. Extensive regions of single-strand DNA formed during replication, and the ATR/Chk1 pathway was over-activated after low UVC doses.

Despras et al. (2010) found that adding a low concentration of caffeine after irradiation lowered Chk1 activation and abolished DNA synthesis in XP-V cells. The Chk1 inhibitor UCN-01 worsened the replication defect in XP-V cells by increasing fork stalling, and like caffeine it made XP-V cells more sensitive to UVC. The authors concluded that pol eta acts at stalled forks to restart them, and that without pol eta, Chk1 becomes essential for replication to resume by alternative pathways through fork stabilization.
